subject: Cloud Computing
title: AWS and the Startup World
description: A quick win: understand AWS and the Startup World.

hook.text: AWS gives startups up to $100,000 in free credits. It's an investment — they're betting you'll grow.

buildup.text: Programs like AWS Activate helped launch thousands of startups that couldn't afford servers.

discovery.text: Airbnb, Slack, and Stripe all started on AWS credits. Free cloud was their launchpad.

twist.text: By the time credits expire, the startup is dependent on AWS. Migrating would cost more than staying.

climax.text: The strategy works brilliantly. Today's credit-fueled startup is tomorrow's million-dollar account.

punchline.text: Free credits today. Loyal customer for a decade.

quiz.question: Why does AWS offer free credits to startups?
options: Startups that grow on AWS become dependent long-term paying customers
AWS is required by law to support small businesses
Credits are only given to companies AWS plans to acquire

details.summary: AWS became the default infrastructure for startups by offering credits programs, pay-as-you-go pricing that scales from zero, and services that eliminate the need for infrastructure teams. Many of the world's biggest tech companies including Netflix, Airbnb, and Slack were built entirely on AWS.
details.whyItMatters: AWS removed the capital barrier to starting a tech company. The startup ecosystem it enabled spawned an entire generation of billion-dollar companies built on cloud infrastructure.
takeaways: AWS credits programs give startups free cloud resources
Pay-as-you-go scales from dollars to millions per month
Netflix, Airbnb, and Slack were all built on AWS

faq.question: How does AWS support startups?
faq.answer: AWS Activate provides startups with credits up to $100,000, technical support, and training. Y Combinator, Techstars, and other accelerators include AWS credits in their programs. This ecosystem ensures that most funded startups begin their cloud journey on AWS.

faq.question: Do startups stay on AWS as they grow?
faq.answer: Many do, because migration costs are high and teams build deep AWS expertise. However, some large companies like Dropbox and Basecamp have repatriated workloads. Others adopt multi-cloud strategies as they grow, adding Azure or GCP for specific capabilities.
